Phase 03 · 7–10 hours

Coil & structure.

Build upward without asking wet clay to carry more than it can. Treat every vessel as a load path, every seam as a relationship, and every pause as a structural decision.

Start with loadSee the vessel brief

Aim

Height through rhythm, not hurry.

Prerequisite

Control pinch-built walls and recognize workable versus leather-hard clay.

By the end

Join coils securely, stage construction, steer profiles, and diagnose cracking, slumping, and twist from evidence.

Deliverables

Seam samples, a profile triptych, a load test, and one 30–40 cm vessel with a failure atlas.

03.1

The vessel is a load path.

At what point does another coil stop adding height and start causing collapse?

Five-beat cycle

Add → consolidate → shape → equalize → rest

Add a coil, integrate it through the wall, establish the intended profile, equalize moisture and thickness, then pause when the lower wall begins to yield.

Read the lower third

New mass travels downward. Bulging, shine, soft ripples, or an ovalizing foot show that the base is losing stiffness. Support, stop, and let moisture equalize—do not hide the warning with more clay.

Lab · Staged load test75 min + pauses
  1. Build three identical 12 cm cylinders. Add one, three, and five coil courses without resting.
  2. Record height, base width, and profile immediately and after 15 minutes. Timing is comparative, not universal.
  3. Repeat with rest decisions based on evidence: lower-wall firmness, reduced tack, and ability to hold the intended silhouette.
  4. Compare deformation. Write the earliest visible warning you missed.
Do not force drying with concentrated heat.Uneven moisture gradients create new stresses. Use loose covering, gentle ambient airflow, and patience appropriate to your studio conditions.
03.2

A seam needs contact, compression, and compatible moisture.

Lab · Seam sampler60–90 min

Make six joined strips. Vary only one condition at a time: equal versus mismatched moisture; dry contact versus minimal slip; light versus firm compression. Label each.

  1. Let samples equalize slowly until firm leather hard.
  2. Flex or section them. Observe whether failure travels through the clay or follows the boundary.
  3. Do not conclude that one joining ritual is universal. Identify the combination that worked for this clay, state, geometry, and pressure.
EvidenceInterpretationCorrection
Crack follows coil lineBoundary remained weak or moisture differedMatch state; improve intimate contact and compression.
Wall thins beside seamIntegration displaced too much claySupport opposite side; use shorter strokes.
Horizontal ridgeCoil attached but not consolidatedBridge material across boundary, then recompress.
03.3

Steer the silhouette course by course.

Place a coil inside the previous wall to narrow, centered to rise, or slightly outside to widen. This is a planning heuristic, not a substitute for supporting and compressing the join.

Study · Profile triptych2 hours

Expand

Widen gradually; track base stability and avoid a sudden shelf.

Rise

Hold a near-vertical load path while resisting twist.

Enclose

Bring coils inward while supporting from inside; preserve access and rim control.

Make three 15 cm studies from equal clay. Photograph every three courses. Annotate placement, pressure direction, and rest points.

TransferChoose one profile and reverse its direction in the upper third. Make the transition feel continuous rather than attached.
03.4

Project: the paced vessel.

Integrated project

A 30–40 cm vessel built in stages.

Use at least one expansion and one enclosure. Keep a build log with course count, profile sketch, clay-state evidence, support used, and reason for each rest.

  1. Draw the intended profile full-size and mark likely high-load zones.
  2. Build a stable base and the first third. Measure width and verticality.
  3. Continue in short cycles. After each, inspect from eye level and overhead.
  4. At leather hard, refine without thinning structural zones. Dry slowly and evenly.
  5. Create a one-page failure atlas: three symptoms, locations, likely causes, tests, and next-build changes.

Inspiration · look comparatively

Coils can declare themselves—or disappear.

Compare a dramatic rim, a large load-bearing body, and a stone-smoothed silhouette. Each uses coiling differently, as documented by the museum records.

Knowledge check · 3 questions

Pause. Predict. Diagnose.

Choose one answer for each situation. Open a hint when needed; explanations appear after you check all three.

Phase checkpoint · 15 points

Can the vessel explain how it stands?

Criterion123
Structural continuitySeams or wall failContinuous wallThickness supports load and profile
PacingBuild outruns clayRest points respond to evidencePacing is documented and anticipatory
ProfileUnintended driftPlanned changes read clearlyTransitions are controlled and lively
DiagnosisGeneric explanationEvidence linked to causeCompeting causes tested
DocumentationIncompleteUsable build logLog supports the next iteration
Pass at 10/15, with no 1 in structural continuity.A structural miss calls for seam samples, not a full remake. A pacing miss calls for the staged-load test.
Retrieval + transfer prompts
  1. Name the five-beat build cycle.
  2. Why can a seam look smooth yet remain weak?
  3. A wall leans only after the sixth course. What evidence would separate an overloaded base from uneven coil placement?
